To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the EEM is greater when emotional stimuli are encoded with neutral stimuli (i.e., in mixed lists) compared to when they are encoded in isolation (i.e., pure lists) and (2) the EEM for emotional stimuli is associated with neural activity in a region of the ventral attention system, while the EEM for neutral stimuli is associated with a region of the dorsal attention system.
the EEM is observed in immediate memory when emotional and neutral pictures are encoded and tested in the same list, but not in separate lists.

the emotional enhancement of memory is observed in immediate memory tests when emotional (negative) and neutral stimuli are presented together (mixed lists) but surprisingly, not if they are presented and tested separately (pure lists), and that the list-composition effect on the emotional enhancement of neutral memory may be due to differential allocation to ventral and dorsal neural networks during encoding.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of attention in memory for emotional information, and the implications of our findings for the neural mechanisms of emotional memory.
the mechanisms of the emotional enhancement of memory (the effect that emotional stimuli are remembered better than neutral stimuli) in humans.
the neural basis of memory for emotionally salient stimuli, and how this is influenced by the context in which they are encoded.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the list-composition effect on memory for emotion and neutral stimuli is due to the differential allocation of attention, with ventral and dorsal networks contributing to the encoding of emotional and neutral stimuli, respectively.
list composition affects the EEM by modulating the contribution of ventral attention to memory for emotional stimuli and dorsal attention to memory for neutral stimuli.

the effect of list composition (mixed versus pure) on the emotional enhancement of memory is due to a differential attentional allocation, with greater ventral attentional allocation to emotional and greater dorsal attentional allocation to neutral stimuli.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EEM is not due to a general attentional enhancement of encoding, but rather to a specific enhancement of encoding for emotional information.
the emotional enhancement effect in memory is due to the differential allocation of attentional resources at encoding.

the emotional enhancement of memory for neutral items occurs when the items are encoded in a list of both neutral and emotional items (mixed list), but not when they are presented in a list of neutral items only (pure list), and that the neural correlates of successful encoding of neutral items differ between the two list conditions, with the ventral and dorsal networks of the attention network playing differential roles.
The main takeaway from our work is that
memory for emotionally salient stimuli is enhanced in a context of mixed emotional and neutral stimuli, but not in a context of only emotional stimuli.
the EEM effect is not a general effect of emotion, but rather, an effect of emotion that occurs in the context of other emotional stimuli.
memory for emotional and non-emotional events may be differentially affected by the presence or absence of other events in memory.
